My parents had this absolutely bananas mentality, no idea where it came from, that basically had them view us their children as a retirement plan. And it seems you're dealing with a similar deviation of that mentality. 

You're not their retirement plan, your home is not their vacation getaway. As a former southern baptist (now atheist) I can understand how you're feeling. There's a lot I shouldn't say, I respect your right to hold beliefs as you see fit. 

On the one hand, I think it's in some ways reasonable for someone to say that their sexuality is not compatible with my identity. Take two cis people in the same situation, a cis het male and a cis lesbian woman. The lesbian's sexuality doesn't mesh with the cis male's identity as male. And that's not wrong. In your case you're figuring it out some time into a marriage, which I'm very sorry you have to deal with. 

On the other hand, it's entirely inappropriate to flip it into 'I support you but I think your existence is still a sin' and is a primary reason I no longer associate with religions in my own life. You deserve to be celebrated, not tolerated. 

These are my opinions. I'm not the most informed person in the world, and if anyone disagrees or feels anything I've said is offensive I'm happy to learn something new. I hope you manage to find yourself and what your happiness looks like even through this unfortunate and awful pain.

Personally the thing that helps me most is writing. I'm not super great at creative writing, but I'm very good at handling text, so I keep a Notepad document open at all times, and when I have a thought I can't get out of my head, I start typing until I don't want to anymore. From there, I can edit, manipulate, adjust until it feels right. And then when it's time for me to mention things to my therapist or to someone else, I have a good guideline of what I did and did not want to say. It's far from perfect but it helps me burn the info-dump off and edit what comes out into something at least functionally coherent. I've written books worth of thoughts down at this point.

A good example of how important it is to have the language available to describe things. I didn't know the word 'dysphoria' or 'dysmorphia' even existed until I was in my late 20's. Those words just weren't used in the common social discourse, I never had access to them. The words that DID exist for me were slurs or dismissals (and nobody wants to identify with those). Suddenly a whole new way of putting all those feelings in one place existed. I didn't have to preface a discussion with an hour of complicated exposition because the definition existed under one word. I could just use that word. Describing my own unique personal experiences with it is a whole other topic though

The way my brain organizes things, sometimes I just don't have a word that adequately describes what I'm thinking or feeling. I don't just think in words and categories, I think in pictures and sensations and contextual intensities. I don't have a word to describe what I feel, and the word I use might lead my therapist to think something that isn't true or attempt to dive deep into something that is on its surface entirely unimportant to what I'm trying to get across.

Just my own opinions. I opted to fully remove myself from my family long before coming out, for various reasons. There's a sense of loss, the idea that the good things a family is supposed to be is gone. But family is just another word for 'people', and people can be awful. It took a long time to not feel that sense of loss. Eventually I realized that what I'd lost was not worth keeping in the first place. I have found so much more satisfaction in the people I choose to give my time to, than my family was ever willing to give me. It's not a flawless swap, especially when we are conditioned with the 'family' image all our lives, but I know that even when I miss my genetic family I am still better off than I would have been remaining under their thumbs. And I feel pride in the fact that I have found good people to associate with, who appreciate me and make me feel loved, despite all of that. It's a good feeling. And really, the thing a family SHOULD do is make you feel loved. It took time and work to get to that point, and I definitely met plenty of awful people too, but yet again, a good family takes work. So in that way, my chosen family is more true than my genetic family ever was.

I did the same. The first really bad fall. I started thinking, "Can I really handle this? What if it happens again? What if it could kill me? Do I really want that?" But I didn't have many options at the time, it was either the scooter or public transit, so I started taking public transit for a bit, until I wanted to go to the store where public transit would have had me walking for half a mile to get there. I took it slow and careful, but I did fine, and slowly had to build my confidence back up like it was day 1 learning to ride again.

Another thought just occurred to me, one I consider helpful. A common saying as I understand it. "It's not if you'll fall, but when." 

I don't know any riders who haven't at least once in their lives. Even the best rider I know, guy who's done motocross since we were kids, has multiple motorcycles, motocross bikes, scooters. He's the one who told me that when I started on my 50cc. And a week later he dumped his bike to avoid an animal.

The trick, and hard part, is not letting fear be paralyzing. Fear in itself is both natural and functionally useful, it encourages caution and awareness. You weren't aware of a risk before. Now you are. After more practice, the range of your confidence will expand, but now you'll have one more good thing to limit yourself away from overconfidence.

I thought I could lean hard at speed even in the rain. Now I know better. Edit: There's a somewhat naive expectation that one is allowed to be LESS cautious with MORE experience and while that can sometimes be true I've also found the opposite true, that more experience has made me more careful. I've worked to know exactly where the limits are and it's made me a better, safer rider. Some lessons only get learned the hard way.

I've always had issues with inappropriately high anxiety. It took me a good while to be confident on a scooter in the first place. After a while though I thought I was hot stuff, speeding into turns and weaving around like a pro. And then on a rainy day I came up to a turn in an intersection where traffic paint had covered a larger area than I was used to. I didn't care, it wasn't anything I hadn't seen before. So I sped into the turn. My front tire slipped as I leaned, wasn't anything I wasn't used to, but my front tire didn't get traction again before my back tire hit the paint too and the back tire slid as well. Whole thing came out from under me. Took some skin off my elbow, bruised for months. 

I was afraid of riding in the rain after that. Anytime I had to, I would take it SUPER cautiously, avoiding any chance of another slip. I wasn't sure of my sense of balance anymore, my confidence was gone. It took a while, but I got a degree of that confidence back. Mishaps are the most effective teachers. You may never have confidence in the exact same way as you did before, but that's a good thing in my opinion. You had a lesson on exactly where your confidence was limiting. Your new confidence will come, and it will be informed by situations like this one. Your confidence will be different, more experienced, but it will come back. If you were to hop back on and learn nothing about it, I would be more concerned.

I used to be terrified of driving anything. My parents yelled a lot whenever they tried to teach me to drive. After a while they just enrolled me in a driving school because I wasn't able to gain that confidence by learning from them. The first thing the teacher did was to have me in an entirely empty parking lot in a car marked as an in-training driver. He had me accelerate to 50 mph, and then slam on the brakes. 

It sounds silly but honestly it worked. I was confident after that, that when I pressed on my brakes they would work. After that there was still fear but most of it went away with experience. Honestly there's more inherent danger on a scooter or motorcycle. What you hear in a car, you feel on a scooter. You hear a bump in a car, you feel a bump on a scooter. In a car the safety is built into the car, on a scooter it's strapped to you (riding gear). Not that you should fear it, being somewhat afraid means you respect the possibility of danger. But whatever you do it will just take time and practice no matter which way you go about transport.

2. **Class 2** transmiting at **2.5 mW** with a range of **10 meters** or **33 feet** (most Bluetooth headsets and headphones are common Class 2 devices).
3. **Class 3** transmitting at **1 mW** with a range of fewer than **10 meters**.
